items.stem: What is the word for a cost or benefit that falls on someone outside the deal between a buyer and a seller?
choices: Opportunity cost
Deadweight loss
Externality
Transaction cost

items.stem: What is the term for the full cost to society of making one more unit, counting both the producer's own cost and the harm to others?
choices: Marginal private cost
Marginal social cost
Marginal external cost
Average total cost

items.source: Ch 17 four types of externalities (new example)
items.stem: Your neighbor keeps bees to sell honey, and the bees also pollinate the fruit trees in your yard. What kind of externality is this?
choices: Negative production externality
Positive consumption externality
Negative consumption externality
Positive production externality

items.source: Ch 17 'Not zero: pollution, crime, even homicide'
items.stem: The chapter points out that highway speed limits could be set at 20 miles per hour. What point does it use this example to make?
choices: Preventing the last bit of harm has real costs, so the best level of harm is rarely zero
Drivers ignore the delay they add for others, so roads end up more crowded than they should be
Safety rules usually cost more than they save, so they should be kept to a minimum
Buyers and sellers can usually fix externalities on their own without any help

items.stem: In the chapter's opening, a buyer and a seller both say yes to a trade. What goes wrong when that trade has an externality?
choices: The buyer pays more for the good than it is really worth to them
The seller hides some of the good's true costs from the buyer
Someone affected by the trade never got a say in it
The government sets a price that is too low for the seller

items.source: Parallel to Market Failures common quiz Group 6.1 #20-21 (paper mills); Ch 17 DWL shortcut and 'DWL is not the damage' misconception
items.stem: Runoff from a chemical plant does $15 of damage downstream for every ton the plant makes. The market produces 120 tons a week, but the efficient quantity is 90 tons. What is the deadweight loss each week?

items.source: Ch 15 Elasticity; parallel to Elasticity quiz Group 2 #27 and #31 (total revenue test)
items.stem: A movie theater raises ticket prices by 10 percent, and ticket sales fall by 25 percent. What happened to the theater's total revenue, and what does that tell you about demand?
choices: Revenue rose, so demand is elastic
Revenue fell, so demand is inelastic
Revenue rose, so demand is inelastic
Revenue fell, so demand is elastic

items.source: Ch 7 Taxes (Unit 1); parallel to Government Intervention and Efficiency quiz
items.stem: Back in Chapter 7, why does a tax on a good create deadweight loss?
choices: Some trades that would have helped both buyer and seller no longer happen
The government tends to spend the tax money less carefully than buyers would
Sellers pass the entire tax on to buyers in the form of higher prices
Buyers pay a higher price on every unit they still choose to buy

items.source: Ch 9 Costs (Unit 2); Unit 2 memorization quiz 'marginal curve rule'; parallel to Production and Costs quiz #62; exam's most-missed idea
items.stem: A firm's average total cost is $18. The next unit it makes has a marginal cost of $14. If the firm makes that unit, what happens to its average total cost?
choices: It rises, because making more output always raises total cost
It stays the same, because fixed costs don't change with output
It falls, because the new unit costs less than the current average
It rises, because marginal cost goes up as a firm produces more

choices: Yes
No
